seoDescription: Gain a solid foundation in rotational motion physics with this introductory guide. Learn the fundamental differences between linear and rotational motion, and master the core concepts of angular position, angular displacement (Δθ), and angular velocity (ω). This video explains how to calculate the average angular velocity in radians per second and explores its relationship to linear velocity. You'll also understand the concepts of period, frequency, angular acceleration, and how they relate.

chapters.title: Introduction to Rotational Motion
chapters.description: Introduces the concept of rotational motion and contrasts it with linear or translational motion.

chapters.title: Angular Position and Displacement
chapters.description: Explains angular position and angular displacement (Δθ) by drawing a parallel to linear position and displacement, and introduces radians as the standard unit.

chapters.title: Understanding Angular Velocity (ω)
chapters.description: Defines average angular velocity (ω) as the rate of change of angular displacement over time and compares its units (rad/s) to linear velocity.

chapters.title: Relating Linear and Angular Velocity
chapters.description: Introduces the formula v = ωr and uses an example to demonstrate that while angular speed is constant on a rigid rotating object, linear speed increases with the radius.

chapters.title: Period and Frequency in Rotation
chapters.description: Defines the period (T) as the time per cycle and frequency (f) as the cycles per second, providing their formulas and units.

chapters.title: Calculating Angular Velocity with Period and Frequency
chapters.description: Presents the key equations that relate angular velocity to frequency (ω = 2πf) and period (ω = 2π/T).

chapters.title: Angular and Linear Acceleration
chapters.description: Defines average angular acceleration (α) by comparing it to linear acceleration, outlining its formula and standard units (rad/s²).

chapters.title: Centripetal (Radial) Acceleration
chapters.description: Explains that any object in circular motion experiences centripetal acceleration, which points to the center, and derives its formulas (ac = v²/r and ac = ω²r).

chapters.title: Tangential and Net Acceleration
chapters.description: Covers tangential acceleration for non-uniform circular motion and shows how to find the net acceleration using the vector sum of centripetal and tangential components.

summary:
## Core Concepts: Rotational vs. Linear Motion

- **Linear Motion**: An object moves from one point to another in a line (also called translational motion).
- **Rotational Motion**: An object rotates or spins around a fixed axis.

> [!TIP]
> Many concepts in rotational motion have direct analogs in linear motion. Thinking of the linear counterpart can help you remember the rotational formula.

## Key Rotational Quantities

- **Angular Position (θ)**: A point on a circle, analogous to linear position. Measured in angles.
- **Angular Displacement (Δθ)**: The change in angular position (Δθ = θ_final - θ_initial). The standard unit is **radians**.
- **Angular Velocity (ω)**: How fast an object is spinning. It is the rate of change of angular displacement.
  - *Formula (Average)*: `ω = Δθ / Δt`
  - *Units*: `radians/second`
- **Angular Acceleration (α)**: The rate of change of angular velocity.
  - *Formula (Average)*: `α = Δω / Δt`
  - *Units*: `radians/second²`

## Relating Linear and Angular Motion

The bridge between linear (tangential) and angular quantities is the radius (r).

- **Linear Velocity (v)**: `v = ω * r`
- **Tangential Acceleration (a_t)**: `a_t = α * r`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> For a rigid rotating object, the **angular velocity (ω)** is the same for every point on the object. However, the **linear velocity (v)** is not; it increases as the distance from the center (radius) increases.

## Period (T) and Frequency (f)

- **Period (T)**: The time it takes to complete one full rotation or cycle.
  - *Formula*: `T = Total Time / Number of Cycles`
  - *Units*: `seconds/cycle`
- **Frequency (f)**: The number of rotations or cycles that occur per unit time.
  - *Formula*: `f = Number of Cycles / Total Time`
  - *Units*: `Hertz (Hz)`, which is `1/s` or `cycles/second`.

These are related to angular velocity with the following key formulas:

- `ω = 2πf`
- `ω = 2π / T`

## Types of Acceleration in Circular Motion

An object moving in a circle can have two components of acceleration.

#### 1. Centripetal Acceleration (a_c)

- Also called **radial acceleration**.
- It is always present if an object is moving in a circle, even at a constant speed.
- It is responsible for changing the *direction* of the velocity vector.
- **Direction**: Always points toward the center of the circle.
- **Formulas**: `a_c = v² / r` or `a_c = ω² * r`

#### 2. Tangential Acceleration (a_t)

- This component is only present if the object's *speed* is changing (i.e., it is speeding up or slowing down).
- It is responsible for changing the *magnitude* of the velocity vector.
- **Direction**: Tangent to the circular path.
- **Formula**: `a_t = α * r`

#### Net Acceleration

When an object is speeding up or slowing down in a circular path, it has both centripetal and tangential acceleration. Because these two vectors are always perpendicular, the magnitude of the **net acceleration (a_net)** can be found using the Pythagorean theorem:

- `a_net² = a_c² + a_t²`
transcription:
## Introduction to Rotational Motion

In this video, we're going to talk about rotational motion. So what exactly is rotational motion? From the word, you can describe that it's any object that can rotate or spin. So that's rotational motion. It's different from linear motion where an object simply moves forward. Linear motion and translational motion basically means the same thing.

## Angular Position and Displacement

Now, what terms do you need to be familiar with when dealing with rotational motion? Well, in linear motion, you have things like position and displacement. For instance, let's say if this is a number line and an object is currently at position a. So position is basically a point in space. Displacement is the change in position. Let's say if the object moves from x_a to x_b, then the object's displacement is the difference between x_b and x_a. It's the final position minus the initial position, that's displacement.

Well, for rotational motion, we have the same terms. There's angular position and angular displacement. So angular position, just like regular position, is a point on the circle. Let's call this point A. And let's say as the wheel spins, the object moves from point A to, let's say, point B. So this angle represents the angular position, and this is also the angular position. But the difference between those two points, I guess you can call it delta theta (Δθ), this is the angular displacement. It's the difference between those two points in a circle. It's the final angular position minus the initial angular position. So that's angular displacement.

Now, the standard unit for angular displacement is the unit radians. Now you can use degrees or any type of angle measure, but the most common unit that you're going to see is radians.

## Understanding Angular Velocity (ω)

Now the next term that you need to be familiar with is angular velocity. Angular velocity tells you how fast an object is spinning on a circle, whereas linear velocity tells you how fast it's moving forward.

So the average linear velocity, or let's say average linear speed, is distance divided by time. Velocity is really displacement over time, but the units will still be meters per second. Now, angular velocity, which is represented by the symbol omega (ω), this is going to be average angular velocity. It's equal to the angular displacement divided by the time. And as you can see, the equations are very similar.

So for average velocity, we have units such as meters per second. And for average angular velocity, it's radians per second. So here, this is going to be displacement over time to get velocity. And to get angular velocity, it's angular displacement over time.

## Relating Linear and Angular Velocity

Now the equation that connects linear velocity to angular velocity is this equation: linear velocity is equal to omega times r.

So whenever you have an object spinning, the angular speed is the same everywhere on a circle. However, the linear speed is not the same. So let me give you an example that will illustrate this. So let's say this is the center of the circle, and this circle is spinning at 5 radians per second. So let's say this is point A and this is point B. Let's move point B to this position.

So which one has the greater angular velocity, point A or point B? Now, because the wheel is spinning at one angular speed, every point on this wheel will travel at that same speed. It's going to rotate at that same rate. So the angular velocity of A is equal to the angular velocity of point B. They're going to rotate at the same rate.

Now what about the linear velocity? Is it the same or is it different? Now, they all spin at the same rate, but point A has a shorter distance to travel. Point B has to travel a longer distance, and in order to spin at the same rate, B has to travel faster than A. So therefore, the linear speed of point B is greater than the linear speed of point A. And there's an equation that we can use, it's this one: v is equal to omega times r. So as r increases, the linear velocity will increase. So notice that r_a is less than r_b. So that's one reason why the linear velocity of B is greater than the linear velocity of point A.

## Period and Frequency in Rotation

Now there's some other terms that you need to know, and that is the period and the frequency. The period is the time it takes to complete one cycle. So if you have the total time and the number of cycles that will make, or rotations, if you divide these two, you're going to get the time it takes to make one complete cycle, or one full rotation around the circle.

Frequency is the reciprocal of period. It's the number of cycles that occurs per second. So if you have the number of cycles and you divide it by the time, this will give you the frequency. So the unit for period is the seconds, but it's really seconds per cycle or seconds per revolution. The unit frequency is hertz, or one over seconds.

## Calculating Angular Velocity with Period and Frequency

Now, period is one divided by the frequency. You can also calculate the angular velocity if you know the frequency. The angular velocity is equal to 2πf. So this is one equation that you want to commit to memory. And you also want to know this one as well. Now if you have the period and you want to calculate the angular speed, you can use this equation: omega is equal to 2π divided by T. So make sure you know those three equations that can relate angular velocity with period and frequency.

## Angular and Linear Acceleration

Now the next thing that we need to talk about is angular acceleration and linear acceleration. So linear acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the change in time. So this is average linear acceleration.

The average angular acceleration is equal to a very similar equation. It's the change in angular velocity divided by the change in time. The units for linear acceleration is meters per second squared. For angular acceleration, it's radians per second squared, at least that's the standard unit. It's rare that you'll see degrees per second squared but that would still be a form of angular acceleration, but this is the most common unit.

## Centripetal (Radial) Acceleration

Now whenever you have an object moving in circular motion, there's different types of accelerations that you need to be familiar with. So if the object has any kind of speed, if it's moving around a circle, it's going to have a centripetal acceleration. And that centripetal acceleration points towards the center of the circle.

The centripetal acceleration is equal to the linear speed squared divided by the radius of the circle. And we know that v is equal to omega r. So the centripetal acceleration is going to be (ωr)² divided by r. So you can cancel one of the r's. So just to take it one step at a time, once you square ωr, you're going to have ω² times r², which is r times r. And then you can cancel one of these. So the centripetal acceleration is ω² times r.

So that's the acceleration that points towards the center of the circle. So if an object is moving with constant speed around a circle, the only acceleration it has is the centripetal acceleration, also known as the radial acceleration. So the net acceleration of the object will equal a_c if it's moving with constant speed.

## Tangential and Net Acceleration

Now what if it's not moving with constant speed? What if it's accelerating around a circle? So then it's going to have a tangential acceleration. And the tangential acceleration is equal to the angular acceleration times r. And we also found the tangential acceleration using this equation: it's the change in velocity divided by the change in time.

Now notice that these two vectors, they're perpendicular to each other. So if we have the centripetal acceleration going this way, and this is the tangential acceleration, therefore the net acceleration of the object at this instant is going in the northwest direction. So when the object is not moving with constant speed around a circle, the net acceleration is the vector sum of the centripetal acceleration and the tangential acceleration. So basically it's the hypotenuse of the right triangle.
